specAnchors.text: understand how to classify a substance as an element, compound or mixture

primer.text: You already know from States of Matter that every substance is built from particles. This note uses that idea to sort every substance into one of three families — an element, a compound or a mixture — by asking two questions: are the atoms all of the same kind, and are any different kinds chemically joined?

modules.title: Elements and Compounds
modules.opening: Every substance in chemistry belongs to exactly one of three families: an element, a compound or a mixture. This lesson takes the two families whose particles are chemically joined — elements, where every atom holds the same number of protons, and compounds, where two or more different elements are bonded into something new that behaves as one substance.
keyPoints: All substances fall into exactly one of three classes: element, compound or mixture.
An element is made of atoms that all hold the same number of protons.
The periodic table holds 118 elements, for example copper, iron and magnesium.
A compound joins two or more different elements by chemical bonds into one substance.
No physical method can split a compound back into the elements it contains.

low.restatement: Everything is either an element (one kind of atom), a compound (different atoms bonded) or a mixture (things merely placed together). Elements cannot be broken into anything simpler; compounds cannot be undone by physical means.
low.analogy: Think of building bricks: an element is one brick type, a compound is bricks glued into a fixed model, and a mixture is a drawer of loose and glued pieces shaken together.
low.examPointer: Quote both halves of the element definition: one proton count throughout, and nothing simpler can be got out of it.

medium.restatement: An element keeps one proton count in every atom, so no chemical or physical process can free anything simpler from it. A compound is different elements reacted together into one substance whose parts cannot be pulled apart by filtering, magnetising or evaporating.
medium.analogy: A compound is like a cake: eggs and flour have reacted into something new, and no sieve will hand you the eggs back. A mixture is still the separate ingredients sitting in one bowl.
medium.examPointer: Classification questions usually turn on one phrase — chemically combined. Write it for compounds, and withhold it for mixtures.

modules.title: Mixtures and Classification
sourceHeadings: Particle diagram showing elements, compounds and mixtures
modules.opening: A mixture is what you get when two or more substances — elements, compounds or both — share a space without chemically joining. Because no bonds form, ordinary physical methods such as filtration or evaporation can pull the ingredients apart again, and particle diagrams make the contrast visible: bonded units of one kind signal a compound, while several different units loose in the same frame signal a mixture.
keyPoints: A mixture holds two or more substances in one place without chemical bonds between them.
The ingredients of a mixture can be elements, compounds or both at once.
Physical methods such as filtration or evaporation separate mixtures into their parts.
Sand in water, oil in water and sulfur mixed with iron filings are all mixtures.
In particle diagrams, a mixture shows different atoms or molecules sharing the space unbonded.

low.restatement: A mixture is substances sitting together, not bonded together. Because the ingredients keep their separate identities, filtering, evaporating or other physical tricks recover each one unchanged.
low.analogy: It is a bowl of mixed nuts: almonds and cashews share the bowl, stay themselves, and you can pick them apart by hand.
low.examPointer: The examiner rewards the phrase chemically combined — attach it to compounds, and withhold it from mixtures.

medium.restatement: Two or more substances count as a mixture whenever no chemical bonds link them, so each keeps its own melting point, appearance and behaviour. Filtration or evaporation then works, because separating a mixture breaks no bond at all.
medium.analogy: Breakfast cereal with nuts and raisins is a mixture: every piece keeps its crunch, and picking the raisins out costs patience, not chemistry.
medium.examPointer: For diagram questions, count the atom types first: one kind means element, one bonded kind means compound, several kinds together means mixture.

glossary.definition: A substance whose atoms all hold the same number of protons and that cannot be split into anything simpler.
A pure substance made of two or more different elements chemically combined.
The chart of all 118 elements, on which every element has its place.
Two or more substances sharing a space without chemical bonds between them.
A physical method that separates an insoluble solid from a liquid by passing the mixture through paper.
A physical method that separates a dissolved solid from its liquid by turning the liquid to gas.
A drawing that uses spheres to show the atoms or molecules present in a sample.
